Backtest: does the 12 °C line move with the physics?

Early August 2026 · a documented wind-driven upwelling event, checked against independent buoy truth and shown as before/after threshold maps.
Verdict: the line moves the way the physics demands. Aug 3 was warm and dead calm (buoy 6 m = 16.5 °C, 0 h west wind). 16 h of west wind then drove the buoy 6 m temperature down to 8.0 °C, and 7.7 °C by Aug 5. The 12 °C isotherm crossed the buoy's 6 m sensor on Aug 4 in both the buoy and the corrected model — timing the model got right. At Silver Harbour the modelled line marched shoreward as the event built (raw isotherm 10 → 7 → 2 m, Aug 3→5), widening the reachable cold-water zone. (Silver's outer-rock shoals hold cold water in cast range on both days, so this spot doesn't flip — it deepens or shoals; a flatter shore would flip.)

Silver Harbour — calm day vs upwelling day

Honest limits. The model tracks the big transition, but not every day: on Aug 2 LSOFS ran warm (16.6 °C) while the buoy was already cold (9.8 °C), a genuine miss. The subsurface correction is state-dependent — smallest on calm days, largest mid-event — so day-to-day isotherm depth carries the ±band shown, not false precision. The buoy is 90 km away in the western basin; Thunder Bay's shore feels the same wind but responds on its own timing. Bathymetry: CHS NONNA-10. Surface: GLSEA. Subsurface truth: NDBC 45027.
